meta.title: Who really said "Spare the rod, spoil the child"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not scripture. The wording is Samuel Butler's, from the 1664 satire Hudibras — a joke about whipping Cupid. Proverbs 13:24 says something else entirely.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Spare the rod, spoil the child'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is not in the Bible. It is a couplet from Samuel Butler's Hudibras (1664), where the "child" being spanked is Cupid.

answer.label: Not the Bible — actually Samuel Butler
answer.sourceLine: The line is a couplet from Butler’s mock-heroic satire Hudibras ↗, Part II, Canto I: “Love is a boy by poets stil’d; / Then spare the rod and spoil the child.” In Butler it is a dirty joke — a widow arguing that the knight deserves a whipping, since the poets call Cupid a boy — and it has nothing to do with raising children. No verse of the King James Bible contains the sentence; the nearest, Proverbs 13:24 ↗, reads “He that spareth his rod hateth his son.”

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: Title page dated 1664; copies were on sale in London by December 1663

source.excerpt:
If matrimony and hanging go
By dest’ny, why not whipping too?
What med’cine else can cure the fits
Of lovers when they lose their wits?
Love is a boy by poets stil’d;
Then spare the rod and spoil the child.
trail: The verse people mean. Proverbs 13:24 in the King James Version ↗ reads “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.” It is not the proverb, and it does not contain the word “spoil.”

1664 — the sentence appears. Butler’s Hudibras, Part II carries an 1664 title page, though it was in the shops by December 1663 ↗, when Pepys bought his copy. In Canto I the widow’s speech on whipping ends: “Then spare the rod and spoil the child.”
1835 — an editor annotates it. T. R. Nash’s edition prints the couplet and glosses the variant reading: “Spoil, or spill, as in some copies” ↗ — an old sense of the word meaning to ruin or destroy.

The reference works agree. The Phrase Finder calls Butler “the coiner of the version that we use in everyday speech” ↗, while pointing out that the proverbial notion is far older — Langland’s Piers Plowman (dated there 1370–90) has “Who-so spareth ye sprynge, spilleth his children.”
source.excerptNote: Text as transcribed in the Project Gutenberg edition (London, 1805). Spellings vary between printings — other editions give “styl’d” for “stil’d,” and T. R. Nash’s 1835 annotated edition notes at this exact couplet: “Spoil, or spill, as in some copies … frequently used by Chaucer, in the sense of, to ruin, to destroy.”

author.name: Samuel Butler
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.metaLine: baptized 1613 – 1680 · English poet and satirist, author of Hudibras
author.bio: Samuel Butler (baptized 14 February 1613, died 25 September 1680) was an English poet and satirist, the son of a Worcestershire farmer, and is remembered almost entirely for one book. Hudibras — a mock-heroic poem of more than 11,000 lines about a preposterous Cromwellian knight and his squire, loosely modelled on Don Quixote — delighted Restoration royalists and stayed more or less continuously in print from the 1660s until the First World War. Its jangling octosyllabic couplets were imitated so widely that the verse form is still called Hudibrastic, and the poem seeded English with phrases most speakers now assume came from somewhere older and holier.

The nearest biblical wording, Proverbs 13:24 (KJV), is "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes." — verified at quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most confidently misquoted sentences in English. It is quoted in sermons, parenting arguments and courtrooms as a Bible verse, and it is not one.

items.why: No verse of the King James Bible contains it. The verse people mean, Proverbs 13:24 ↗, reads “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.” No “spoil,” no if-then. Wiktionary ↗ notes that the “spoil” concept is absent from the Bible, which is precisely why the phrase more likely came from Butler.

The thought really is biblical — Proverbs 23:13–14 ↗ is blunter still. That overlap is what lets the substitution pass unnoticed: people recognise the sentiment and assume they recognise the sentence.
The Phrase Finder observes that the phrase is often assumed to be Victorian ↗ because it sounds like Victorian self-improvement. It was already in print in the Restoration.

items.who: Everyone who quotes it about children
items.why: In Butler’s poem ↗ the line sits inside a comic argument for flogging a lovesick knight. “Love is a boy by poets stil’d” — so the child to be spanked is Cupid, not anybody’s son.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Samuel Butler’s, from Hudibras ↗, Part II, Canto I, whose title page is dated 1664. The Bible supplied the idea; a Restoration satirist supplied the sentence.

context.heading: How a joke about whipping Cupid became parenting scripture
lead: The couplet arrives at the least pious moment imaginable. Hudibras, Butler’s ridiculous Puritan knight, has been locked in the stocks and bailed out by a rich widow on one condition: he must flog himself. In Part II she presses the bargain, and runs through a mock-scholastic defence of whipping — whipping as “Virtue’s governess,” whipping as the cure for lovesickness — before landing the punchline. The poets call Love a boy; so spare the rod and spoil the child. The “child” is Cupid.

What travelled was the couplet, stripped of its setting. Butler’s line is short, rhymed and memorable in a way that Proverbs 13:24 is not, and it says roughly what that verse says, so English speakers quietly filed a Restoration satirist’s gag under scripture. The result is a sentence quoted in arguments about discipline for three and a half centuries by people who believe they are quoting the Bible, and who would be startled to learn they are quoting a joke about spanking the god of love.
context.detailsSummary: What the Bible actually says about the rod
detailsBody: Two passages in Proverbs supply the idea. Proverbs 13:24 (KJV): “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.” Proverbs 23:13–14 (KJV): “Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die. Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell.”

Neither uses the word “spoil,” and neither has the proverb’s if-then shape. Wiktionary makes the point plainly: the “spoil” concept is not in the Bible, which is why the wording more likely came from Butler.

The proverbial notion is much older than Butler in English. The Phrase Finder cites William Langland’s Piers Plowman, dated there to 1370–90: “Who-so spareth ye sprynge, spilleth his children” — where “spilleth” carries the older sense of ruin or destroy. What Butler contributed was not the thought but the sentence.
context.pull: The “child” in the proverb is Cupid.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Project Gutenberg text of Hudibras contains the lines "Love is a boy by poets stil'd; / Then spare the rod and spoil the child" in Part II, Canto I, with marginal line numbers placing them at 843–44; the ebook is a transcription of an edition published in London, 1805.

The 1835 T. R. Nash annotated edition prints "Then spare the rod, and spoil the child" and carries a footnote reading "Spoil, or spill, as in some copies, from the Saxon, is frequently used by Chaucer, in the sense of, to ruin, to destroy."

Wiktionary states the phrase is commonly claimed to come from Proverbs 13:24, but that "due to the associated 'spoil' concept which is not in the Bible, it more likely came from a 17th-century poem by Samuel Butler called Hudibras", in which a love affair is likened to a child and spanking is mockingly commended.

The Phrase Finder states "The coiner of the version that we use in everyday speech was Samuel Butler, in Hudibras", notes the phrase is often wrongly assumed to be Victorian, and cites Langland's Piers Plowman (1370–90): "Who-so spareth ye sprynge, spilleth his children."

Wikipedia's Hudibras article states the poem was published in three parts in 1663, 1664 and 1678; that Part Two bore the date 1664 and Pepys bought a copy on 10 December 1663; and that while the original proverb appears in Proverbs 13:24, "this poem is the first appearance of the quotation and popularised the aphorism 'spare the rod and spoil the child'."
Wikisource's King James Bible text of Proverbs 13:24 reads "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes."

Bible Gateway's KJV text gives Proverbs 23:13–14 as "Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die. Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell."
Wikiquote's Samuel Butler (poet) page quotes "Love is a boy by poets styl'd; / Then spare the rod and spoil the child" and cites it to Hudibras, Part II, Canto I, line 843.
Wikipedia states Samuel Butler was baptized 14 February 1613 and died 25 September 1680, and was an English poet and satirist remembered chiefly for Hudibras.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation — a site search for the exact phrase "spoil the child" returns "Nothing Found", so there is no QI anchor finding to defer to.
